prompt: It is January 2, 2019. I would like to outperform the S&P 500 over the next five years. Can you propose 10 stocks I should buy? Answer as of that date.
reply:
# 10 Stocks to Beat the S&P 500 (as of January 2, 2019)

**A caveat first:** I'm answering from 2026, so I already know how 2019–2023 turned out, and I can't fully set that aside. Any list I build will likely lean toward names that did well. Treat this as an illustration of reasoning from January 2019, not as evidence that the approach works. It isn't personal financial advice.

---

## Where things stand (January 2, 2019)

- **The market just fell hard.** The S&P 500 dropped about 20% from its September peak to its December 24 low. It ended 2018 down about 6%, its worst year since 2008.
- **The worries are rates, trade and politics.** The Fed raised rates again in December, to 2.25–2.50%. The US–China trade war is escalating, and the government is partly shut down.
- **Valuations have reset.** The index trades at about 14–15x forward earnings, and many high-quality growth stocks are 20–50% below their 2018 highs.

**The strategy:** buy durable, cash-generating businesses with long growth runways while they're on sale, then hold them for five years.

## The 10 picks

| # | Company | Why own it | Key risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Microsoft (MSFT)** | Azure is growing about 75% a year, and Office 365 subscriptions are replacing one-time license sales. It just became the world's most valuable company. | Cloud price competition with AWS and Google |
| 2 | **Alphabet (GOOGL)** | It dominates search, owns YouTube, has cloud upside and holds about $100B in net cash. | Antitrust and privacy regulation |
| 3 | **Amazon (AMZN)** | AWS is growing about 45% with high margins, and advertising is a new profit engine. | Heavy spending, regulatory scrutiny |
| 4 | **Apple (AAPL)** | It's down about 35% from its October high and trades near 13x earnings. Services revenue is growing, and it buys back a lot of stock. | Weaker iPhone demand, especially in China |
| 5 | **Visa (V)** | It earns a toll on the global shift from cash to cards, with very high margins and little credit risk. | Fintech disruption, fee regulation |
| 6 | **UnitedHealth (UNH)** | It's the largest US health insurer, and its Optum services arm is growing fast. Earnings have been steady through downturns. | "Medicare for All" politics ahead of 2020 |
| 7 | **Adobe (ADBE)** | Creative Cloud subscriptions give it recurring revenue and pricing power. It's expanding into marketing software (Marketo, Magento). | Its valuation is already high |
| 8 | **Costco (COST)** | Its membership model, with about 90% renewal, has held up well against Amazon and in recessions. | Thin margins, rich valuation |
| 9 | **Thermo Fisher (TMO)** | It's the largest supplier of life-science tools, and most of its revenue is recurring. It benefits from growth in biotech research. | Integrating acquisitions, debt |
| 10 | **NVIDIA (NVDA)** | It's the higher-risk contrarian pick: down about 50% after a crypto-driven inventory glut. Its datacenter chips for AI are growing more than 50%. | Semiconductor cycles, more inventory write-downs. *This is also the pick most open to my hindsight bias.* |

## How to hold them

- **Equal-weight the positions** at about 10% each and rebalance once a year, so no single stock dominates.
- **Expect more volatility than the index.** Ten stocks are concentrated, and this list leans heavily toward tech. Beating the S&P 500 requires being different from it, and being different can also mean falling behind for long stretches.
- **Hold through downturns.** Most of the expected edge comes from buying quality at a discount and not selling in the next correction.
- **Mind costs and taxes.** Use a tax-advantaged account where possible and trade rarely.

---

If you'd like, I can step out of 2019 and check how this list actually did against the S&P 500 from January 2019 to January 2024. The index roughly doubled over that period, including dividends.
